import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 197

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/197](https://www.erdosproblems.com/197)
-/

open Set

namespace Erdos197

/--
Can $\mathbb{N}$ be partitioned into two sets, each of which can be permuted to avoid monotone
3-term arithmetic progressions?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem erdos_197 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ A B : Set ℕ, IsCompl A B ∧
      (∃ f : ℕ ≃ A, ¬HasMonotoneAP (Subtype.val ∘ f) 3) ∧
      (∃ g : ℕ ≃ B, ¬HasMonotoneAP (Subtype.val ∘ g) 3) := by
  sorry

end Erdos197

reformulations.difference: The bijections `ℕ ≃ A` and `ℕ ≃ B` require both partition classes to be infinite, whereas the source merely says 'two sets'.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Finite classes cannot occur in a valid partition. If one class were finite, the other would contain every integer beyond some N. In any enumeration of that cofinite class, let a be the first value at least N, and b the first value greater than a. Then a precedes b, and c = 2b − a belongs to the class and must occur after b, yielding an increasing three-term AP. Thus both classes are necessarily infinite, and their ordinary one-sided permutations are precisely bijective enumerations by ℕ. The converse is immediate. A full equivalence with a formulation allowing either finite permutations (`Fin n ≃ A`) or ℕ-indexed permutations was proved as `Review197.finite_classes_irrelevant` in `/workspace/review/scratch.lean`.
